misconceptions.belief: A weight is added to its input, and turning it down only adds less.
misconceptions.truth: A weight multiplies its input; below zero the product is negative and pulls the sum down.

misconceptions.belief: The output is the inputs passed through, added or averaged; the dials are decoration.
misconceptions.truth: Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added.
The sum is made before the valve; the gauge shows what passes.

misconceptions.belief: One click moves the needle by the same amount on every dial.
misconceptions.truth: One click moves the sum by that dial's input times the click; a bigger input moves it further.

misconceptions.belief: The output can be any number, including below zero.
misconceptions.truth: The valve stops every sum below zero, so the output rests at zero.

misconceptions.belief: Each input has its own valve (the valve acts before the sum).
misconceptions.truth: The products are added first; the valve acts once, on the sum.

misconceptions.belief: The miss is the size of the gap, or the output minus the target.
misconceptions.truth: The miss is the target minus the output, with its sign: positive means the output must rise.

misconceptions.belief: To fix the output, change the input.
misconceptions.truth: Inputs are given; tuning changes only the weights.

misconceptions.belief: Each example gets its own dial setting.
misconceptions.truth: One setting serves every example; tuning looks for the setting that meets all of them.

misconceptions.belief: There is exactly one right setting.
misconceptions.truth: Several settings can meet every mark.

misconceptions.belief: There is always a setting that meets every mark.
misconceptions.truth: Contradictory examples leave a smallest total miss above zero.

sentences.text: {machine}This is Plate One: a drawing of a machine that turns numbers into one number.
{neuron}A machine like this is called a neuron.|
{purpose}Neurons wired together by the billions are what AI systems are built from; this plate draws one.
{tubes}Numbers go in on the left, drawn as blue liquid in these two glass tubes.
{input}Each number that goes in is called an input.|
{x1}The first tube holds the first input, and its value is written at the end of the tube.
{x2}The second tube holds the second input.
{scale}Read an input on the scale under its tube: the liquid ends at its value.
{other}Other inputs fill the tubes to other levels: here the first tube is full, and the second is empty.
{back1}Now the tubes go back to the first inputs.
{given}Inputs come from outside the neuron; nothing inside it changes them.
{recap1}So far: a neuron, and two inputs held in two tubes.
{dials}Each input flows out of its tube through a dial, drawn as a red knob on a scale.
{weight}The setting of a dial is called a weight: it says how much its input counts.|
{multiply}The dial multiplies its input by its weight.
{stays}The input stays in its tube; the dial makes a new number from it.
{product}That new number, the input times the weight, is called the product.|
{note}The working is written in the note, one line per step.
{one}Turn the weight to one: the product equals the input, so the input passes as it is.
{three}Turn it higher: now the product is three times the input.
{half}Turn it between zero and one: the product is smaller than the input.
{zero}At zero the product is zero, whatever the input: this input no longer counts.
{neg}Below zero the product is negative, drawn as flow running backward.
{recap2}A weight multiplies its input: above one the product is larger than the input, between zero and one smaller, at zero it is zero, and below zero it is negative.
{back2}Turn the first dial back to its first setting.
{dial2}The second input has its own dial, and its own weight.
{p2}Its product is made the same way: the second input times the second weight.
{chamber}Both products flow into this chamber, drawn as a glass column.
{dashed}The dashed line across the column marks zero.
{sum}The chamber adds the products, and the total is called the sum.|
{signs}A positive product raises the level, and a negative product draws liquid out, so the level drops.
{newin}Keep the dials, and give the neuron new inputs.
{cancel}Now the two products are equal and opposite, so the sum is zero.
{further}Turn the second dial further below zero.
{wins}Its product is now further from zero than the first product, so the sum is below zero.
{recap3}Each input times its weight, then all the products added: that is the sum.
{meets}After the chamber, the sum reaches a part that lets flow go forward only.
{valve}This part is called a valve: a sum above zero passes, and a sum below zero is stopped.|
{gauge}The needle on this gauge shows what passes; here nothing passes, so it stays at zero.
{output}The gauge reads the output: the one number that comes out.|
{stopped}Here the sum is below zero, so the valve is shut, and the output is zero.
{differ}The sum is below zero and the output is zero: they are not the same number.
{back}Keep the dials, and give the neuron new inputs.
{passes}The sum is above zero, so the valve opens, and the output equals the sum.
{graph}This graph draws the valve: the sum along the bottom, the output up the side.
{flat}Below zero the line lies flat at zero; above zero it rises with the sum.
{bend}So the line has one bend, at zero.
{recap4}The output comes after the valve: when the sum is below zero, the output is zero; when the sum is above zero, the output equals the sum.
{target}The output we want is called the target: the right answer for these inputs, given with them.|
{mark}It is drawn as this brass mark on the gauge.
{miss}The gap from the needle to the mark is called the miss.|
{minus}The miss is the target minus the output: start at the needle and go to the mark.
{pos}Here the needle is below the mark, so the miss is positive: the output must rise.
{negm}Turn the first dial up: the needle passes the mark, and the miss is negative, so the output must fall.
{onmark}Turn the second dial down a little: the needle sits on the mark, and the miss is zero.
{recap5}The target is the output we want; the miss is the target minus the output, with its sign.
{again}Start again: new inputs, a new target, and both dials at zero.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {tuning}Changing the weights to bring the output to the target is called tuning.|
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {locked}Only the dials turn: the input tubes are locked.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {case}An input is the case in front of the neuron; changing it would answer a different question.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {own}The dials are the only part that belongs to the neuron, so tuning turns only the dials.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {recap6}Tuning turns only the dials; the inputs are given to the neuron.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {start}Both dials are at zero, so the output is zero, and the miss is positive.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {click}Each turn of a knob to the next mark on its scale is called a click.|
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {rise}A positive miss means the output must rise, so turn the first dial up.
note: valve: 0.0 is not above 0, so output 0.0

sentences.text: {c1}One click: the product grows, and the miss gets smaller.
{c2}Another click, and the miss gets smaller again.
{c3}A third click is too far: the needle passes the mark, and the miss is negative.
{short}The first dial alone cannot land on this mark: one click short, or one click past.
{size}Each click of the first dial moves the needle twice as far as a click of the second, because its input is twice as big.
{pull}So turn the second dial one click below zero.
{met}The needle is on the mark, and the miss is zero: the neuron is tuned for these inputs and this target.
{recap7}Tuning by hand means: read the miss, turn a dial the way that makes it smaller, and repeat.
{example}A set of inputs together with its target is called an example.|
{four}Here are four examples. Their inputs wait in a rack on the left, sets one to four, and each has its own target.
{onebyone}The machine runs one example at a time: {s1}set one, {s2}then two, {s3}then three, {s4}then four, and each output lands on its own small gauge.
{lamps}Under the dials, one lamp per example lights while its needle is on its mark: the setting is right only when all four are lit.
{oneset}The neuron has one set of dials, and that one setting serves every example.
{nomark}Once tuned, the neuron is given new inputs that have no brass mark.
{suit}It answers them with the one setting it has, so that setting must suit every example.
{firstok}With the setting tuned by hand, the first example has its needle on its mark.
{others}The other three needles are off their marks.
{worked}Load set two into the machine: its output falls well short of its target.
{moveall}Turn the second dial up one click to help it, and the machine runs all four examples again, one after another: every needle moves.
{broke}The first needle leaves its mark, the fourth lands on its mark, and the third moves further away.
{recap8}One setting serves every example, and a turn meant for one example moves them all.
{putback}Put the second dial back one click.
{sizes}The size of a miss is the miss without its sign.
{total}The total miss adds the four sizes, and the tally under the gauges adds them up.
{plate3}Plate Three measures many misses more carefully.
{tuner}A tuner is a procedure that turns the dials by itself.|
{step}At each step it turns every dial a little, so that the total miss gets smaller.
{twogrow}Here two misses shrink, and two grow.
{offclick}The tuner is not held to the clicks: it can turn a dial by part of one.
{run}Step by step, the total miss shrinks, until every miss is almost zero.
{lit}Every needle now sits on its mark, near enough that all four lamps light.
{plate5}How the tuner works is drawn on Plate Five.
{recap9}A tuner turns every dial a little each step, and the total miss gets smaller.
{learning}Tuning the weights from many examples, with a tuner, is called learning.|
{never}Learning turns only the dials; the inputs stay locked.
{pullnet}Wire many neurons together, so that the outputs of some become the inputs of others,
{network}and you have a neural network.|
{billions}Large networks have billions of dials.
{tuned}Nobody sets them by hand: a tuner sets them, until the outputs are as close to their targets as one setting allows.
{recap10}Many neurons, wired together and tuned from examples, make a neural network that learns.

sentences: {d1}Your turn. Take the first dial, and turn it two clicks up.
{d1ok}The needle rose: the first input now counts.
{d1hint}Drag the first dial, or press the right arrow key twice.
{d2}Now turn the second dial until the needle sits on the brass mark.
{d2ok}On the mark. Chapter Seven met this same mark with another setting: one example can be met in more than one way.
{d2hint}The needle is below the mark, so the second dial goes up.
{d3}New inputs, and a new mark. Set both dials yourself.
{d3ok}On the mark, with no help.
{e1a}Set the first dial so that its product will match the goal written in ink, then press the knob in.
{e1b}The first dial is locked. Bring the sum down to its goal with the second dial.
{e1ok}Matched.
{e1miss}Not this product. The note shows the input times your weight.
{e1n}The product is the input times the weight. Below zero, the product is negative.
{e2}Place one pencil where the sum will be, and one where the needle will land, then lift the cover.
{e2ok}Both marks are right: the sum, then the output after the valve.
{e2miss}A mark is off. The note now shows every step for this case.
{e2n}Multiply each input by its weight, add the two products, then apply the valve.
{e3}The arrow shows which dial will turn, and how many clicks. Place the pencil where the needle will land, then press it in.
{e3ok}The needle lands on your mark.
{e3miss}The needle lands away from your mark. The note shows how far each click moved the sum.
{e3n}One click moves the sum by that dial's input times one click; below zero, the needle stays at zero.
{e4}Get the needle as low as you can, then press Done.
{e4b}The needle rests at zero. Turn the dials until it leaves zero, and watch the sum.
{e4ok}Watch one more click: the sum falls again, and the needle stays at zero. The valve lets nothing below zero through.
{e4okb}The sum had to climb past zero before the needle could move.
{e4miss}The needle can still go lower.
{e4n}Watch the sum and the needle together as the sum crosses zero.
{e5}Build the neuron from its parts, then run the three test examples.
{e5ok}All three needles meet their marks. The products are added first, and the valve acts on the sum.
{e5miss}A test needle missed its mark. Follow one example through your machine.
{e5n}Each input goes through its own dial first; the chamber adds; the valve comes after everything is added.
{e6}Turn the dial until the miss is the value written in ink, then press the knob in.
{e6ok}That is the miss.
{e6miss}Not this miss. The miss is the target minus the output.
{e6n}Start at the needle and go to the mark: up the scale is positive, down is negative.
{e7}The needle is off its mark. Put it on the mark.
{e7ok}On the mark, and the inputs are as they came.
{e7n}Only the weights can change. The inputs are given.
{e8}Two examples, one set of dials. Put both needles on their marks.
{e8ok}Both needles on their marks, with one setting.
{e8n}A click moves each needle by its own input times the click, so the two needles move by different amounts. Turn the dial that moves the far needle more.
{k2}Plate B has a larger input. Set its dial so that its product reads the same as plate A.
{k1}Same inputs, different dials, different needles. Turn plate B's dials until both needles read the same.
{k9}Both needles read zero, but the sums differ. Turn plate B's second dial until its sum matches plate A.
{k8}Plate B's first dial turns one click up. Turn plate A's first dial until its needle has moved as far as B's.
{k3}Plate A's needle is above zero; plate B's rests at zero. Turn plate B's second dial up until its needle leaves zero.
{k4}The same example flows through both builds. Move plate B's valve until both needles read the same.
{k5}Plate A's needle is below its mark; plate B's is above. Turn plate B's dial until its miss equals plate A's.
{k6}Plate B got a larger input. Using only plate A's dials, make A read the same as B.
{k7}Both plates show the same two examples. Plate B meets both marks. Make plate A meet both, with one setting.
{r2}It looks like a weight adds to its input. It does not. It multiplies the input, and below zero it makes the product negative.
{r1}It looks like the inputs pass straight through. They do not. Each input is multiplied by its weight, then the products are added.
{r10}It looks like the gauge shows the sum. It does not. The sum is made before the valve; the gauge shows what passes.
{r11}It looks like every click moves the needle the same distance. It does not. A click moves the sum by that dial's input times the click.
{r3}It looks like the needle can go below zero. It cannot. The sum goes below zero; the valve stops it, so the output rests at zero.
{r4}It looks like each input has its own valve. It does not. The products are added first, and the valve acts on the sum.
{r5}It looks like the miss is the size of the gap, or the output minus the target. It is the target minus the output: start at the needle and go to the mark.
{r6}It looks like the input is the thing to change. It is not. An input is the case in front of the neuron; only the weights are turned.
{r7}It looks like each example gets its own setting. It does not. One setting serves both; look for where both needles land together.
{r8}It looks like there is one right setting. There is not. Each lettered pair of ticks meets every mark.
{r9}It looks like some setting must meet every mark. None does. Two examples with the same inputs want different outputs.
{skip}Three right on the first try. You can be the tuner now, or keep working here.
{t0}You are the tuner now: your job is to make the total miss small.
{col}Four examples, one setting. The tally on the right adds up the four misses.
{job}Turn the dials until every needle sits on its mark.
{t1}Four new examples. Tune the dials until every needle sits on its mark.
{thint}The second dial moves needles two and four the most.
{l1}Every needle on its mark.
{l2more}Now find a different setting that also puts every needle on its mark.
{l2}Each lettered pair of ticks meets every mark: there is more than one right setting.
{l3go}This time, get the total miss as small as you can, then press Done.
{l3more}A smaller total is still on the clicks. Keep tuning.
{l3}Two examples have the same inputs and different targets. No setting meets both, so no total miss reaches zero.
{ttuned}You read the misses, turned the dial that shrank them, and did it again.
{tuning}That is tuning: you were the tuner.
{payoff}One neuron: inputs times weights, added, through a valve, tuned until its misses are as small as one setting allows.
{line}Drawn against the first input, one neuron's output is a line that bends once.
{marks}These marks need a line that bends twice.
{question}What if the answer needs two bends?
{close}One neuron bends its line once; the next sheet wires several together.
Thanks for tuning with me.
See you there.
